title: National statistics vs human judgement
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou explains how scaled scores from Comparative Judgement can be mapped to a standard, and compares two ways of setting it: national statistics and teacher judgement. With large, nationally representative samples, the same share of top grades is awarded as on the national test, so grading is never harsher or more generous than the national system. Where such data is missing, teachers are asked where the standard should sit and the answers are averaged, as in a New Zealand assessment. Her main point is that how you set the standard matters less than how you maintain it, since statistics produce quotas and human judgement produces swings. Comparative Judgement addresses this by linking assessments through carried-over samples of work.
points: Comparative Judgement yields a reliable scale, but teachers still need to know what a scaled score means against a national grade.
Statistical standard-setting guarantees consistency with national grading in large, representative samples.
Teacher judgement can set a new standard when national data is unavailable, by averaging disagreeing views.
Maintaining a standard over time is the harder problem, and linking assessments through shared samples of work holds it constant.
quotes: If you use Comparative Judgement for an assessment, it will provide you with a very reliable and robust measurement scale. Here is an example: if you comparatively judge 100 pieces of student writing, you will get a scaled score for each one.
At this point, the most common question people have is this: how does that scaled score match up to a national standard? If a student has a scaled score of 520, what does that mean?
We use this approach for most of our big assessments. It means that our grading is never harsher or more generous than the national system.
The other option is to use human judgement to draw a line on the distribution. Ask your teachers: where do you think the standard should go? They won’t all agree, but you can take an average.
Actually, it doesn’t matter too much how you set the standard. What really matters is how you maintain the standard going forward.

If you use statistics, you risk ending up with grade quotas that don’t recognise true improvement (or regression!) across a cohort. If you use human judgement, you risk getting very inconsistent results and wild swings from one year to the next.

With Comparative Judgement, you can easily link assessments over time by pulling forward a sample of responses from one assessment to the next. This allows us to place all our assessments on the same consistent scale - and therefore to hold the standard the same too.
